about: Oldest and most remarkable natural things of the isles (research track, 2026-10-22): ancient trees, ancient woods, oldest rocks, fossil sites, early human traces and natural wonders. Each entry: the age claim, how well it is established, and sources with exact quotes (checked by python -m bidb.evidence --check).

entries.name: Fortingall Yew
entries.age_text: estimated 2,000–3,000 years by many; Forestry and Land Scotland say c. 5,000; suggestions range from 1,500 to 9,000
entries.claim: possibly the oldest living tree in Britain and one of the oldest in Europe
entries.evidence: No ring count is possible (the heartwood has gone); ages come from the girth of 56 ft recorded in 1769–71 and growth-rate assumptions, so estimates span 1,500 to 9,000 years.

sources.title: Fortingall Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Some estimates put the tree's age at between 2,000 and 3,000 years

sources.title: Fortingall Yew (Wikipedia)

sources.quote: Others have suggested an age as great as 5,000 to 9,000 years

sources.title: Fortingall Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

entries.name: Llangernyw Yew
entries.age_text: often given as 4,000–5,000 years; alternative view c. 1,500 years
entries.claim: one of the oldest trees in Wales
entries.evidence: The 4,000–5,000-year figure comes from a 2002 Yew Tree Campaign certificate (David Bellamy); the trunk is fragmented and there is no scientific dating of the tree itself; others tie it to the Christian site (c. 1,500 years).

sources.title: Llangernyw Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: its age is unclear but probably over 4,000 years old

sources.title: Llangernyw Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: which would make it around 1,500 years old

entries.name: Defynnog Yew
entries.age_text: claimed c. 5,000 years; investigation suggests 2,000–3,000; Ancient Yew Group minimum 1,300 years
entries.claim: claimed to be the oldest tree in Britain
entries.evidence: The 5,000-year claim (Yew Tree Campaign certificate) is not supported by later investigation; the Ancient Yew Group's Toby Hindson gives a projected minimum of 1,300 years.

sources.title: Defynnog Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is considered more likely that the two yew trees are in the order of two to three thousand years old

sources.title: Defynnog Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: gives a projected age on the hard evidence currently held by the AYG of a minimum 1,300 years

entries.name: Crowhurst Yew
entries.age_text: thought to be about 4,000 years (girth estimate; unverified)
entries.claim: one of the oldest yews in England
entries.evidence: The 4,000-year figure is a girth-based estimate; the tree is documented by its 1630 girth measurement and by John Evelyn in 1664, which proves only a large tree by the 17th century.

sources.title: Crowhurst Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is thought to be about 4,000 years old

sources.title: Crowhurst Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Its girth was measured in 1630 as 30 feet

entries.name: Ankerwycke Yew
entries.claim: witness to the sealing of Magna Carta (1215)
entries.evidence: A girth-based range (8 m girth); the Magna Carta association is tradition, but a tree of this size would have been standing in 1215.

sources.title: Ankerwycke Yew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The tree is at least 1,400 years old, and could be as old as 2,500 years

entries.name: Kingley Vale yew forest
entries.location: Kingley Vale, near Chichester, West Sussex
entries.claim: one of Europe's finest yew forests, with some of the oldest living things in Britain
entries.evidence: Ages are girth-based estimates for the largest yews in the grove.

sources.title: Kingley Vale National Nature Reserve (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The forest contains yews as much as 2,000 years old

entries.name: Marton Oak
entries.claim: the widest oak in Britain and probably the oldest
entries.evidence: Age is estimated from girth (the trunk has split into sections; heartwood rotted), so it cannot be ring-counted. Coordinates approximate (village of Marton).

sources.title: Marton Oak (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The tree is believed to be 1,200 years old

entries.name: Bowthorpe Oak
entries.location: Bowthorpe Park Farm, near Bourne, Lincolnshire
entries.age_text: about 1,000 years (estimate); younger than the Marton Oak
entries.claim: commonly called the UK's oldest oak
entries.evidence: The 'oldest oak' label rests on its girth (c. 13 m); the cited source says it is surpassed in age by the Marton Oak (c. 1,200 years) and King Offa's Oak at Windsor.

sources.title: Bowthorpe Oak (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is commonly thought to be the UK's oldest oak tree on account of its size, although it is surpassed in age by the 1,200-year old Marton Oak

entries.name: Major Oak
entries.claim: Robin Hood's tree; Britain's best-known oak
entries.evidence: Girth-based estimate (10 m girth); possibly several fused saplings. The RSPB announced in June 2026 that the tree had died after failing to come into leaf.

sources.title: Major Oak (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Thought to be between 800 and 1,200 years old

sources.title: Major Oak (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In June 2026, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), which manages the forest, announced that the tree had died

entries.name: Tortworth Chestnut
entries.age_text: over 800 years on documentary evidence; legend of a nut planted in 800 AD
entries.claim: one of the oldest sweet chestnuts in Britain
entries.evidence: Documentary references (1664 and 1712 accounts reporting it in the 12th–13th centuries) support 800+ years; the 1150 name and AD 800 planting legend are weaker.

sources.title: Tortworth Chestnut (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: dating it at over 800 years old

sources.title: Tortworth Chestnut (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a legend recounts that the tree sprang from a nut planted in 800 AD

entries.name: Wistman's Wood
entries.age_text: oldest oaks 400–500 years; possibly a relic of woodland that covered Dartmoor c. 7000 BC
entries.claim: a remnant of Dartmoor's primeval forest
entries.evidence: Tree-ring work shows the living oaks are a few centuries old; the link to prehistoric wildwood is a plausible inference, not demonstrated continuity.

sources.title: Wistman's Wood (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The oldest oaks appear to be 400–500 years old

sources.title: Wistman's Wood (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is likely to be a leftover from the ancient forest that covered much of Dartmoor c. 7000 BCE

entries.name: Black Wood of Rannoch
entries.location: south shore of Loch Rannoch, Perth and Kinross
entries.age_text: pinewood descended from the first pines after the last Ice Age (c. 9,000 years)
entries.claim: one of the largest remnants of the ancient Caledonian pine forest
entries.evidence: Native-pinewood remnants are defined as descended from the post-glacial colonising pines; the individual trees are only a few centuries old.

sources.title: Loch Rannoch (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Black Wood of Rannoch, a fragment of the former Caledonian Forest

sources.title: Caledonian Forest (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: directly descended from the first pines to arrive in Scotland following the ice age

entries.name: Fossil Grove
entries.claim: fossil stumps of a Carboniferous forest of lycopsid trees, preserved in place
entries.evidence: Age from the stratigraphic position of the shale (Limestone Coal Formation); well established.

sources.title: Fossil Grove (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The strata were deposited approximately 325 million years ago when the tree-like plants were still alive

entries.name: Lulworth Fossil Forest
entries.location: east of Lulworth Cove, Dorset (Lulworth ranges)
entries.claim: the stumps of a Jurassic conifer forest, preserved as 'algal burrs'
entries.evidence: Age from the Purbeck strata at the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary; the trees themselves survive only as moulds within microbial limestone. Coordinates approximate.

sources.title: Fossil Forest re-opens to the public
sources.author: Dorset National Landscape
sources.quote: The 145 million-year-old ‘forest’ is a key part of the Jurassic Coast’s ‘walk through time’ story

entries.name: Borth submerged forest
entries.age_text: c. 1500 BC on radiocarbon dates (other studies give older dates for parts of the bed)
entries.claim: a drowned prehistoric forest, linked with the legend of Cantre'r Gwaelod
entries.evidence: Stumps of oak, pine, birch, willow and hazel radiocarbon dated; exposed by storms (e.g. Storm Hannah, 2019).

sources.title: Borth (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Radiocarbon dating suggests the trees date from about 1500 BCE

entries.name: Mount's Bay submerged forest
entries.age_text: forest growing c. 6,000 to 4,000 years ago
entries.claim: drowned forest, origin of the Cornish name of St Michael's Mount ('the grey rock in the wood')
entries.evidence: Peat and wood around Penzance are radiocarbon dated.

sources.title: Mount's Bay (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: indicate that the forest was growing from at least 6,000 to around 4,000 years ago when rising sea levels finally killed the trees

entries.name: Hatfield Forest
entries.age_text: medieval royal forest with pollards over 1,200 years old (estimate)
entries.claim: the best-preserved medieval royal forest in England (Oliver Rackham)
entries.evidence: Rackham's historical ecology shows the medieval forest structure survives; tree ages are estimates.

sources.title: Hatfield Forest (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There are over 800 ancient trees in the wood pasture areas, some of which are over 1,200 years old

sources.title: Hatfield Forest (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Hatfield is the only place where one can step back into the Middle Ages

entries.name: Lewisian gneiss
entries.age_text: just over 3,000 million years (protolith ages 3,125–2,800 Ma)
entries.claim: the oldest rocks in the British Isles
entries.evidence: Radiometric (U-Pb zircon) dating summarised by the BGS Geological Conservation Review volume. Point placed at Scourie, a type area.

sources.title: Lewisian, Torridonian and Moine rocks of Scotland, chapter 1
sources.author: British Geological Survey / JNCC (Geological Conservation Review vol. 34)
sources.quote: including the oldest rocks in the British Isles, dated to just over 3000 Ma

sources.title: Lewisian, Torridonian and Moine rocks of Scotland, chapter 1
sources.author: British Geological Survey / JNCC (Geological Conservation Review vol. 34)
sources.quote: with protolith ages between 3125 Ma and 2800 Ma

entries.name: Inishtrahull Gneiss
entries.claim: the oldest rock in Ireland
entries.evidence: Radiometric dating of the Rhinns complex gneiss (also on Islay and Colonsay).

sources.title: Inishtrahull (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is dated at 1.7 billion years old, making it Paleoproterozoic in age, and is the oldest known rock on the Irish Islands

entries.name: Malvern Hills Precambrian rocks
entries.claim: among the oldest rocks in England
entries.evidence: Radiometric dates on the Malverns Complex; the cited source gives both 670 and 680 million years.

sources.title: Malvern Hills (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the oldest of which are about 670 million years old

sources.title: Malvern Hills (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: which are around 680 million years old

entries.name: Anglesey Precambrian rocks (GeoMôn)
entries.age_text: Precambrian, c. 600–700 million years (the oldest rocks in Wales)
entries.claim: the oldest rocks in Wales
entries.evidence: Anglesey's Mona Complex is Neoproterozoic; ages and order of its groups are still debated (South Stack, once thought oldest, now Cambrian). Point is the island centre.

sources.title: GeoM%C3%B4n (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: solid rocks from the Precambrian to the Neogene

sources.title: GeoM%C3%B4n (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: having been first identified as the oldest Precambrian rock then the youngest

entries.name: Siccar Point (Hutton's Unconformity)
entries.age_text: Silurian greywackes c. 440 million years under Devonian sandstone c. 375 million years; recognised 1788
entries.claim: the unconformity that convinced James Hutton of 'deep time'
entries.evidence: Stratigraphic ages well established; the site's fame is historical (Hutton, Playfair and Hall, 1788).

sources.title: Siccar Point (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Hutton's Unconformity found in 1788

sources.title: Siccar Point (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: are overlain unconformably by gently dipping terrestrial sandstones of late Devonian age

entries.name: Knockan Crag (Moine Thrust)
entries.age_text: older Moine rocks pushed over Cambrian–Ordovician rocks during the Caledonian (Scandian) orogeny, c. 430 million years ago
entries.claim: where older rocks lie on top of younger ones, explained by thrusting (Peach and Horne, 1907)
entries.evidence: The Highlands Controversy was settled by the BGS survey memoir of 1907; the thrust's Scandian age is well established.

sources.title: Knockan Crag (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the Moine schists at the top of the crag appeared to be older than the Cambrian and Ordovician rocks

sources.title: Moine Thrust Belt (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Moine Thrust Belt was formed during the Scandian orogenic phase

entries.name: Charnwood Forest (Charnia)
entries.claim: Charnia, the first Precambrian fossil recognised as such (found 1956–57)
entries.evidence: U-Pb zircon dating of volcanic ash beds in Charnwood; sources give 570–550 Ma for the organism and c. 560 Ma for the rocks.

sources.title: Discovering Charnia
sources.author: Charnwood Forest Geopark
sources.quote: Charnia is key to our understanding of how animals first evolved, more than 560 million years ago

sources.title: Charnia (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Charnia is significant because it was the first Precambrian fossil to be recognized as such

entries.name: Rhynie chert
entries.claim: the oldest land plants and ecosystem preserved with cellular detail
entries.evidence: Older works gave c. 390 Ma; radiometric dating now puts it at about 407–410 Ma. The Geological Conservation Review calls it one of the most important palaeobotanical sites in the world.

sources.title: Rhynie chert (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: formed about 410 million years ago

sources.title: Rhynie (GCR site report)
sources.author: Cleal & Thomas, Palaeozoic Palaeobotany of Great Britain, GCR vol. 9 (JNCC), via Scottish Geology Trust
sources.quote: Rhynie is probably the most important palaeobotanical site in Britain, yielding the oldest known vascular plant fossils with well-preserved anatomical details

entries.name: Valentia Island tetrapod trackway
entries.claim: one of the oldest records of four-legged vertebrates walking
entries.evidence: Age from the Devonian sandstones (dated by stratigraphy, not directly); found by Iwan Stössel in 1992. Some doubt whether all marks are true tracks.

sources.title: Valentia Island & Over the Water Geosites
sources.author: Discover Iveragh
sources.quote: These footprints were left in the sediment around 385 million years ago

sources.title: Valentia Island (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: discovered fossilised tetrapod trackways, footprints preserved in Devonian rocks

entries.name: Wren's Nest
entries.claim: Silurian reef fossils including the 'Dudley Bug' trilobite
entries.evidence: Stratigraphic age of the Wenlock limestone, well established; over 700 fossil types recorded.

sources.title: Wren's Nest (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: which was formed some 420 to 425 million years ago

sources.title: Wren's Nest (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: more than 700 types of fossil have been found at the site

entries.name: East Kirkton Quarry
entries.claim: early land animals including Westlothiana and the oldest known temnospondyl
entries.evidence: Dated by stratigraphy of the Viséan lake deposits.

sources.title: East Kirkton Quarry (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the most fossil-rich layer is dated to around 341 ± 3 million years ago

entries.name: Elgin Reptiles
entries.claim: classic early reptile fossils from building-stone quarries
entries.evidence: Age from the Permian and Triassic sandstones; the fossils survive as natural moulds. Point is Elgin town.

sources.title: Elgin Reptiles (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Elgin Reptiles is the name given to the Permian and Triassic fossils found in the sandstone deposits in and around the town of Elgin

entries.name: Lyme Regis (Mary Anning's coast)
entries.age_text: Early Jurassic (c. 200–190 million years); first famous finds 1811–12
entries.claim: the first correctly identified ichthyosaur skeleton and first near-complete plesiosaurs
entries.evidence: The finds are historical facts; the rocks' Jurassic age is well established.

sources.title: Mary Anning (Wikipedia)

sources.title: Lyme Regis (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

entries.name: Isle of Wight dinosaur coast
entries.location: Back of the Wight (Brighstone–Compton Bay), Isle of Wight
entries.claim: one of the most important dinosaur fossil areas in Europe
entries.evidence: Fossil bones and footprints in the Wealden Group, exposed by cliff erosion. Point approximate (south-west coast).

sources.title: Isle of Wight (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The island is one of the most important areas in Europe for dinosaur fossils

entries.name: Happisburgh footprints
entries.claim: the oldest known human footprints outside Africa
entries.evidence: Dated by palaeomagnetism, biostratigraphy and pollen of the Cromer Forest Bed; the prints were recorded by photogrammetry and washed away within weeks (Ashton et al. 2014).

sources.title: Hominin Footprints from Early Pleistocene Deposits at Happisburgh, UK
sources.author: Ashton N. et al., PLOS ONE 9(2): e88329, 2014
sources.quote: the oldest known hominin footprint surface outside Africa at between ca. 1 million and 0.78 million years ago

sources.title: Happisburgh footprints (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: around 850–950,000 years ago

entries.name: Pakefield
entries.claim: the earliest evidence of humans in northern Europe (until Happisburgh)
entries.evidence: 32 worked flints dated by mammal biostratigraphy and palaeomagnetism (Parfitt et al., Nature 2005).

sources.title: First northern Europeans arrived early

entries.name: Boxgrove (Boxgrove Man)
entries.claim: the oldest human remains in Britain

entries.name: Swanscombe Palaeolithic site
entries.claim: the Swanscombe skull, among the oldest human fossils in Britain

sources.quote: It dates to the Hoxnian interglacial (Marine Isotope Stage 11), around 425-375,000 years ago

entries.name: Pontnewydd Cave
entries.location: Elwy valley, near St Asaph, Denbighshire
entries.claim: the oldest human remains in Wales (early Neanderthal teeth)

sources.title: Red Lady of Paviland (Wikipedia)

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
